newsitem.title: USA: NYC mayor sees debt service rising by FY 1999.
newsitem.headline: NYC mayor sees debt service rising by FY 1999.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani on Thursday unveiled his preliminary financial plan for fiscal 1998, which includes a nearly $18.9 billion four-year capital plan.
The plan would sharply increase the city's cost of debt service, as it would rise to nearly 19 percent in fiscal 1999 from about 16.5 percent in fiscal 1997.
While debt service would ease after that, slipping a few percentage points in 2000, it would climb again by 2002, when the mayor projected it would reach almost 19.5 percent.

The modest increase in capital spending caught the eye of a Standard & Poor's Corp analyst, even though he said his initial reaction was positive, as the city is getting the benefit of strong profits earned by Wall Street firms and using them to help close the over $1.4 billion budget gap projected in fiscal 1998.
"Overall debt levels for the city are high and we're very concerned they're going to get too high," said Martin Arrick, who also pointed to big, out-year gaps as cause for concern.
In fiscal 1999, the Guiliani Administration is projecting an almost $2.4 billion gap, followed by a nearly $3.3 billion gap in 2000.
But Arrick added that at first glance, he did not see anything in the mayor's preliminary plan that would cause him to change the city's rating.
Standard and Poor's rates New York BBB-plus with a stable outlook, he added.
